title: Why do data scientists hate pie charts and how to choose better visuals on Mac
metaTitle: Why do data scientists hate pie charts: selecting better visuals on Mac
description: Learn why data scientists avoid pie charts and how to select effective data visualizations on your Mac without expensive tools.
targetKeyword: why do data scientists hate pie charts
intro: Data scientists often dislike pie charts because they make comparing precise values difficult for the human eye. This bias stems from the fact that our brains struggle to accurately judge area and angles compared to linear positions.
tldr: Pie charts force the brain to estimate angles rather than comparing lengths.
Data scientists prioritize accuracy and clarity over aesthetic trends.
Effective visualization requires choosing the right chart for the specific data type.
You can improve your visuals on Mac using simple design principles and better tools.

blocks.text: The cognitive problem with pie charts

The core issue is cognitive load. When you look at a pie chart, you must mentally calculate the arc length or the central angle of each slice. This is not how our visual system works best. Research shows that we are much faster and more accurate at comparing positions along a common scale, like in a bar chart.

When you use a pie chart, you introduce unnecessary noise. If slices are similar in size, the difference becomes almost impossible to discern. This leads to misinterpretation by your audience. A data scientist aims for truth. A pie chart often obscures it.
Why data visualization selection is a persistent struggle

Choosing the right visual is a balance of analytical accuracy and design. Most data scientists are trained in math or coding, not graphic design. This lack of formal training means many professionals learn by trial and error. It is a tedious process that often leads to inconsistent results.

items: Audience misalignment: Choosing a chart that is too complex for the stakeholder.
Design clutter: Including too many colors or labels that distract from the data.
Misleading axes: Using scales that distort the reality of the trends.

blocks.text: Evidence based fixes for better visuals

You do not need expensive software to fix your visualization workflow. Start by defining the goal. Ask yourself what specific question the chart must answer. If you want to compare values, use a horizontal bar chart. If you want to show a trend over time, use a line chart.

items: Simplify: Remove gridlines and borders that do not add value.
Limit colors: Use a single color for bars and a contrasting color for the key data point.
Label directly: Place labels next to the data instead of using a separate legend.
Sort data: Always sort bars by value unless there is a logical order like time.

blocks.text: Tools for data scientists on Mac

When working on a Mac, performance matters. Many enterprise tools are built for Windows. Always check the official support site before buying. For custom work, Python libraries like Seaborn and Matplotlib are standard. For business intelligence, web-based tools often perform better on macOS than native desktop versions of legacy software.

faq.question: Are pie charts ever useful?
faq.answer: They are acceptable only when comparing a very small number of categories, usually two or three, where the difference in size is massive and obvious.

faq.question: What is the best alternative to a pie chart?
faq.answer: A horizontal bar chart is almost always better because it allows for easy comparison of lengths along a shared axis.
